title: In-Pit Groundwater Management
body: Water in the pit doesn't wait for paperwork — standing water on a haul road or a sump that overtops catches crews flat-footed if nobody's pre-planned the pump route and discharge point. Right now this is only a draft SOP under review, so whatever's protecting ADW from a bad dewatering incident today is informal practice, not an approved procedure.
keyPoints: Before any pump starts: confirm discharge destination, pond capacity, freeboard, and embankment condition. If the receiving pond can't safely take more water, pumping does not start — full stop.
Shift handover must cover sump/pond levels, pump availability, pipeline condition and active discharge route, and any planned mining or blasting that could hit the dewatering system.

Standing water on a road or working area is a stop-work trigger: barricade, notify the shift supervisor, find an alternate route, pump it out to an approved location, repair the surface, then get authorisation before reopening to traffic. Nobody drives or walks into standing water of unknown depth.
Any relocation or modification of pumps, pipelines, or discharge points needs a risk assessment and goes through Management of Change — it's not a "just move it" job.
Maintenance on dewatering gear is LOTO territory: isolate, release stored pressure, verify zero energy before anyone touches it.
apply: If you see pooling near a ramp toe, sump, or low point after any water-cart or rain activity, treat it as a standing-water event under this draft SOP's logic even though it's not signed off yet — barricade and escalate rather than letting equipment thread around it. This SOP is still unapproved, so don't assume a formal sump/pump system is fully in place; check what's actually built versus what's on paper.
